content: The study by Moet et al. (2010) evaluated the effectiveness of a single dose of rifampicin in preventing leprosy among close contacts of newly diagnosed leprosy patients. This was a cluster randomized controlled trial published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The intervention involved administering a single dose of 600 mg rifampicin or a placebo to eligible contacts under supervision, with follow-up conducted over six years. The study demonstrated that single-dose rifampicin significantly reduced the proportion of contacts diagnosed with leprosy within one to two years after enrollment. The COLEP trial, conducted by Moet et al. (2008) and published in BMJ, also assessed the impact of single-dose rifampicin as chemoprophylaxis for leprosy prevention. This trial included 21,711 close contacts of 1,037 newly diagnosed leprosy patients in Bangladesh. The results showed a significant reduction in leprosy incidence among contacts who received rifampicin compared to those who received a placebo. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2012) outlines the methodology for systematic reviews and evidence synthesis. The systematic review conducted for leprosy prevention included randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies assessing immunoprophylaxis and chemoprophylaxis interventions. The search strategy utilized MeSH terms and Boolean operators to identify relevant studies, with no restrictions on study design or language. The systematic review identified 87 citations, of which 19 full-text articles were reviewed. The quality of the included randomized controlled trials ranged from low to moderate. The evidence suggested that BCG vaccination at birth is effective in preventing future leprosy infections compared to placebo or no BCG. Additionally, the combination of single-dose rifampicin and BCG vaccination demonstrated a protective effect of 80%, indicating enhanced effectiveness in individuals who received BCG in childhood. The LPEP study, initiated in 2017, aimed to assess the effectiveness, impact, and feasibility of contact tracing and single-dose rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis. This program was implemented in multiple countries, including India, Indonesia, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Tanzania. The study included leprosy patients diagnosed within two years prior to the start of fieldwork and those diagnosed during the program period. Participants were required to have confirmed leprosy diagnoses, be on MDT treatment for at least four weeks, reside in the pilot area, and have household or neighbor contacts willing to disclose their disease status. The systematic review also evaluated the effectiveness of various vaccines, including BCG, ICRC, and Mycobacterium w, in preventing leprosy. The evidence indicated that BCG vaccination alone or in combination with other interventions, such as single-dose rifampicin or killed Mycobacterium leprae, reduced leprosy incidence. However, data on adverse events and the effectiveness of other vaccines were limited. The review highlighted the need for further research on chemoprophylaxis and immunoprophylaxis strategies for leprosy prevention, particularly in high-risk populations. The findings support the use of single-dose rifampicin and BCG vaccination as effective interventions for reducing leprosy transmission under programmatic conditions.
